entities.name: Rajadhi Rajasinha of Kandy
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Rajadhi Rajasinha II (reigned 1782–1798) was the last fully independent monarch of the Kandyan Kingdom, an ancient Sinhalese monarchy located in the central highlands of present-day Sri Lanka. A member of the Madurai Nayakkar dynasty, he succeeded his elder brother Kirti Sri Rajasinha, inheriting a kingdom increasingly beleaguered by the formidable Dutch East India Company (VOC) on its coastal peripheries. His reign represented the twilight of indigenous sovereignty in Ceylon before the full assertion of European colonial power, making him a pivotal figure in the island's transition from an independent realm to a British protectorate. He is remembered not only for his political struggles but also as a patron of Buddhism and a distinguished poet, reflecting the cultural vibrancy maintained even under duress.

Ascending the throne in 1782 amidst ongoing territorial disputes with the Dutch, Rajadhi Rajasinha initially sought to secure his kingdom's borders and influence. His foreign policy was marked by a pragmatic approach, attempting to leverage the Anglo-Dutch rivalry to Kandy's advantage, particularly during the Fourth Anglo-Dutch War (1780-1784). He engaged in diplomatic overtures with the British, notably through Governor Frederick North, hoping to expel the Dutch from the island, a strategy that ultimately proved unsuccessful in securing Kandy's long-term independence. Domestically, he continued the royal patronage of Buddhist institutions, commissioning new temple constructions and fostering literary pursuits, including his own contributions to Sinhala poetry, one notable example being the 'Asadisa Jataka Kavya'.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Rajadhi Rajasinha's reign marks the final period of full independence for the Kandyan Kingdom before its eventual British annexation, making him a crucial figure in Sri Lanka's transition to colonial rule. His diplomatic efforts to play European powers against each other, though ultimately unsuccessful, represent a last stand for indigenous sovereignty.
